newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Severe water shortage hits Tanzanian capital.
newsitem.headline: Severe water shortage hits Tanzanian capital.

text.p: Drought in Tanzania has caused a severe water crisis in the capital Dar es Salaam, forcing breweries to lower output and prompting a U.N. agency to warn about the danger of waterborne diseases breaking out.

"We are getting very concerned. Definitively we are worried that there might be some breakout of waterborne diseases because we don't know how the people are cleaning the water now and whether that's enough," a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Health Organisation told Reuters on Tuesday.
"We don't know what we actually can do at the moment, it's a very difficult situation."
Health officials said residents on the outskirts of Dar es Salaam were so desperate in their search for water that they had started using water contaminated with faeces and urine.
The drought, caused by low rainfall around December, has severely reduced water levels in the Ruvu river south of Dar es Salaam which supplies the city of three million people.
It was not immediately known if the drought had affected Tanzania's main export crops including cotton, coffee and tea.

"Save water. The city of Dar es Salaam is currently facing a huge water shortage and we would therefore be most greatful if you could help us by saving water whenever possible," said a notice posted in the lobby of Dar es Salaam's Sheraton Hotel.
Several breweries said they faced imminent closure.

"We are down to about 50 percent of our normal production capacity. We are drilling our own boreholes now but within the next week to 10 days it's possible that we will have to stop production completely," Danie Niemandt, the South African chief executive director of the Tanzania Breweries Ltd in which South African Breweries has the biggest stake, told Reuters.
"If we don't get any water tomorrow (Wednesday) we'll have to stop production," Ken Nieuwenhuizen of the Coca-Cola bottling plant in Tanzania told Reuters.
"If we haven't got any water we'll have to close and until the rains come we won't get any water and there is not much we can do. It's bad -- our production is reduced significantly."
An official at the ministry of water said the government had launched a special action plan to cope with the water crisis, but gave no details of the plan.
